title: Twitter Trending Topics (Streaming Analytics)
problem: Design a real-time trending topics / hashtag system over a 500M-tweets/day firehose.
summary: A streaming analytics pipeline that ingests tweets into Kafka, runs Flink jobs that maintain Count-Min Sketch + heavy-hitter Top-K per sliding window, and surfaces results via a small hot-topic cache behind a read API. The dominant design choice is approximate sketches (CMS + Top-K heap) over exact counting — exact counts would require O(unique-terms) memory per window and cross-node shuffles on every update, while CMS gives ε-bounded counts in kilobytes with single-pass updates. The main tradeoff is accuracy at the long tail: heavy hitters are correct within a few percent, but low-frequency terms have noisy counts that aren't trustworthy.

functional: Ingest tweets from a Kafka firehose at 5.8K QPS sustained and 18K peak
Extract hashtags and tokens per tweet and feed them into the sketch
Maintain a 5-minute sliding window, refreshed every 10 seconds
Expose a global top-K (K=50) and a per-country top-K (K=20)
Serve trending reads from a hot cache with p99 under 100ms
Allow on-demand inspection of the underlying term counts for debugging
nonFunctional: Approximate counts with ε ~ 0.1% error at the 99% confidence level
At least 99.9% availability on the read path
Bounded memory per stream task (CMS fits in a few MB per window)
Horizontal throughput scalability by Kafka partition count
Tolerate stream processor restarts with at most ~1 minute of re-read from Kafka
Back-pressure on Kafka producer cannot block the user-visible tweet write path

assumptions: 500M tweets/day, avg 2 hashtags per tweet → 1B hashtag tokens/day
Trending window: 5 min sliding, updated every 10s
Top-K output: K=50 globally, K=20 per country
estimates: Token QPS through Flink: 2x tweet rate ≈ 12K–36K tokens/sec
CMS size per window: 4 hashes * 2^20 counters * 4B ≈ 16 MB — trivial per Flink task
Hot topic cache: 50 topics * few KB = KB-scale; 10M reads/day → ~120 RPS

architecture.mermaid: graph LR client[Client UI] --> api[Trending API] api --> cache[(Hot Topic Cache)] ingest[Tweet Ingest API] --> kafka[Tweet Stream] kafka --> flink[Stream Processor] flink --> cms[CMS + Top-K State] flink --> cache

client.name: Client UI
client.summary: Web/mobile app that renders the trending panel.

sections.heading: Responsibilities
sections.body:
- GET /trending?country=... on panel open
- Poll or WebSocket for updates every 30–60s (doesn't need to be second-fresh)

sections.heading: Why this matters for beginners
sections.body: Trending is eventually-consistent and can tolerate seconds of staleness — very different latency budget from a chat or checkout path.

bottlenecks.title: Polling stampede on breaking-news events
bottlenecks.trigger: During a Super Bowl / election-level event, 3x burst in active users all hit GET /trending on panel open; with a 30–60s poll interval and millions of concurrent clients, request rate can spike from ~120 RPS baseline into the tens-of-thousands RPS range
bottlenecks.symptom: Trending panel shows spinner or stale data; CDN origin fetches surge, Trending API 5xx rate climbs, and users retry-tap making it worse
bottlenecks.mitigation: Add client-side jitter (±25%) to the 30–60s poll interval to decorrelate clients; use a WebSocket push channel for active panels so only the server decides push cadence; respect Cache-Control max-age=30 from the CDN so tab-switch doesn't refetch
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on Trending API RPS > 10x rolling baseline within 1 min, and on CDN origin-fetch ratio climbing above 5% (CDN hit ratio should stay >95% for a 30s-cached JSON)

bottlenecks.title: Stale trending due to client not knowing pipeline freshness
bottlenecks.trigger: Flink job lag or checkpoint-recovery (≤60s re-read from Kafka) causes cache writes to pause; client keeps rendering the last JSON with no indication of staleness
bottlenecks.symptom: Users see a frozen trending list for minutes during an active news event — exactly when they expect it to move fastest — and complain the product is broken
bottlenecks.mitigation: Include a server-provided generated_at timestamp in the /trending response; client renders a subtle 'updated Xs ago' label and auto-refreshes aggressively (every 10s) when staleness > 90s; hide the panel entirely if staleness > 5 min
bottlenecks.detection: Client-side RUM metric on (now - generated_at) p95; alert when p95 > 120s for >2 min across a region

bottlenecks.title: Oversized payload on low-bandwidth mobile clients
bottlenecks.trigger: Response includes 20 topics × sample_tweets each; at a few KB per sample tweet this can balloon to 50–100KB per poll, polled every 30–60s → ~1–2 MB/hour just for trending on a phone
bottlenecks.symptom: Elevated data usage complaints, slow panel render on 3G/Lie-Fi, p99 client render latency well above the 100ms target (mostly network time, not server time)
bottlenecks.mitigation: Lazy-load sample_tweets only when a topic is expanded (return just {topic, rank, score, delta_pct} in the list call); enable gzip/brotli at the CDN; cap limit=20 server-side and reject larger requests
bottlenecks.detection: RUM histogram of /trending response size and TTFB by network type; alert when p95 payload > 20KB or mobile p95 render > 500ms

prebuild.explanation: ### Why the Client UI is called out here For a trending-topics system on a 500M-tweets/day firehose, the Client UI is where the *latency budget* gets decided. Unlike a DM or a checkout, a trending panel doesn't need to reflect the firehose second-by-second — users accept a list that's 30–60 seconds stale. Calling out the client in the design makes that contract explicit: the client polls (or holds a WebSocket) on a slow cadence, which lets every component downstream — API, Redis, Flink — be sized for a trickle of reads instead of a real-time push to millions of devices. ### What happens if you don't design the client deliberately If every open app aggressively refetched `/trending` on tab focus with no jitter, a breaking-news moment (Super Bowl, election call) produces a *polling stampede*: millions of clients hit the Trending API within the same second, the CDN origin-fetch ratio spikes, Redis connection counts climb, and users see spinners exactly when they most want the panel to work. The failure cascades backward from a component most designers don't think of as "infrastructure." ### The number Baseline read load is `10M reads/day ÷ 86,400s ≈ 120 RPS`. A 3× burst with correlated polling (everyone refreshing at once) can multiply that by 100× into the 10K+ RPS range. Client-side jitter on the poll interval and a 30s CDN cache on the JSON turn that burst back into something the 2-replica API can serve comfortably. ### The trade-off The designer accepts visible staleness (a subtle "updated 45s ago" label) in exchange for a read path that costs almost nothing to run.

ingest.name: Tweet Ingest API
ingest.summary: Receives tweet events (from the core Twitter write path) and emits them to Kafka.

sections.heading: Scope
sections.body: In a real Twitter, tweets already exist in a write pipeline; this API is the adapter that publishes to the analytics Kafka cluster.

sections.heading: Event shape
Backpressure
sections.body: If Kafka write is slow, drop to a local disk buffer (3 min retention) rather than blocking the tweet write path. Analytics must never stall user-visible tweeting.

bottlenecks.title: Kafka producer backpressure stalls the tweet write path
bottlenecks.trigger: Kafka broker slowdown, partition leader election, or network blip while sustaining 5.8K tweets/sec (18K peak); synchronous acks=all producer calls begin queuing and the in-memory producer buffer (default 32MB) fills within seconds at 18K msgs/sec
bottlenecks.symptom: Tweet Ingest API p99 latency climbs from ~10ms into seconds, upstream tweet-write callers see timeouts, and if the adapter is inline with user writes, users cannot post tweets — an analytics pipeline taking down the product
bottlenecks.mitigation: Use async producer with acks=1 (not all) for analytics-grade durability, enable the documented 3-min local disk spool buffer, and hard-timeout the Kafka send at 50ms — on timeout, write to disk buffer and return 200 to caller so analytics never blocks user writes
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on producer buffer-available-bytes < 20% for >30s, on record-send-latency p99 > 50ms, and on disk-spool-bytes > 0 (any spillover is a signal the hot path is degrading)

bottlenecks.title: Disk spool buffer overflow during extended Kafka outage
bottlenecks.trigger: Kafka cluster unavailable for >3 min during peak 18K tweets/sec; at ~1KB/tweet that's 18MB/sec, so a 3-min retention spool fills with ~3.2GB per ingest node and older events get dropped
bottlenecks.symptom: Silent data loss in analytics — trending topics go flat or miss a breaking-news spike because the tweets that would have driven it never reached Flink; no user-visible error since ingest returned 200
bottlenecks.mitigation: Size local spool disk for 15 min retention (~16GB at peak) not 3 min, emit a structured drop-log for every evicted event, and have a replay job that re-publishes spooled events to Kafka in order once the cluster recovers with a dedup key on tweet_id
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on spool-disk-usage > 50% for >1 min, on spool-eviction-count > 0 (should always be zero in steady state), and on Kafka producer connection-count dropping to 0

bottlenecks.title: Hashtag-parse and payload-validation CPU cost at 3x burst
bottlenecks.trigger: Peak burst (3x sustained) pushes ~18K tweets/sec through the adapter; each tweet requires UTF-8 decode, hashtag regex extraction, and JSON serialization — at ~3–10ms service time per tweet the documented concurrency=5000 gives headroom but a bursty 54K/sec spike (3x of 18K peak) saturates CPU
bottlenecks.symptom: Ingest API CPU pegged at 100%, service time drifts from 10ms toward the top of the range, and horizontal autoscaling lags by 60–90s causing a brief queue buildup and elevated 5xx on the /ingest endpoint
bottlenecks.mitigation: Precompile hashtag regex once per JVM, move hashtag extraction downstream into Flink's FlatMap (ingest just forwards the raw tweet), and set HPA on CPU>60% with min 3 replicas so scale-out starts before saturation
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on ingest CPU > 70% for >2 min, on service-time p99 > 15ms, and on request-queue-depth > 100 per replica

prebuild.explanation: ### Why there's a separate Ingest API in front of Kafka For a trending system riding a 500M-tweets/day firehose, the analytics pipeline is a *guest* on top of Twitter's real write path. Users don't tweet to get onto trending — they tweet to post. The Ingest API exists as an **adapter and shock absorber** between the tweet write path and the analytics Kafka cluster. It reshapes raw tweet events into the `{tweet_id, hashtags, country, created_at}` shape Flink wants, and — critically — it's where we put the rule "if Kafka is slow, spill to local disk; never block the user." ### What happens without it Without this seam, you'd have two bad options. Either the core tweet-write service talks to Kafka directly (now a Kafka broker hiccup or partition leader election stalls user-visible tweeting — an analytics pipeline taking down the product), or Flink reads from the main tweet storage (coupling analytics replay/backfill to the write-path database). With the Ingest API in place, a Kafka outage manifests as spooled events on local disk and a PagerDuty alert for the data team, not a spinner when users tap "Tweet." ### The number Sustained load is `500M / 86,400 ≈ 5.8K tweets/sec`, with 3× bursts to ~18K/sec during events like the Super Bowl. At ~1KB per tweet, that's 18MB/sec of inbound traffic — the local disk spool sized for 15 minutes holds ~16GB, buying the ops team a real window to recover Kafka without dropping events. ### The trade-off The designer accepted an extra hop (and its ~3–10ms latency) to keep analytics failures strictly isolated from the user write path.

kafka.name: Tweet Stream (Kafka)
kafka.summary: Durable, partitioned tweet firehose feeding downstream analytics.

sections.heading: Partitioning
sections.body: Random partition (not by user or hashtag) so hot hashtags don't create hot partitions. Flink's keyBy does the grouping downstream.

sections.heading: Retention
sections.body: 24h hot; analytics jobs can replay a day if they fail or need to backfill a new sketch config.

sections.heading: Throughput
sections.body: 18K peak tweets/sec on 50 partitions — ~400/sec per partition, comfortably within Kafka limits.

lost: Lower throughput per shard (1MB/s) vs a tuned Kafka partition

bottlenecks.title: Consumer lag during 3x burst exhausts partition parallelism
bottlenecks.trigger: Peak bursts (Super Bowl, elections) push ingest to ~18K tweets/sec across 50 partitions = ~360 msgs/sec/partition; if Flink parallelism lags (GC pause, checkpoint stall, rebalance), per-partition backlog grows at full ingest rate since Flink parallelism is pinned 1:1 to partitions (50 subtasks)
bottlenecks.symptom: Trending panel freezes or shows a 2–5 min old list during exactly the breaking-news moment users care about; Flink consumer-lag metric climbs into the millions of records, and cache-write watchdog fires the 2-min staleness alert
bottlenecks.mitigation: Over-provision partitions to 100–150 (not 50) so Flink can scale parallelism up during bursts without a repartition; enable Kafka's fetch.max.bytes tuning and Flink's unaligned checkpoints so a slow subtask doesn't stall the whole job; pre-warm Flink task managers before known events
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on kafka_consumergroup_lag > 500K messages for >60s, on max-per-partition lag > 50K, and on Flink's currentEmitEventTimeLag > 30s

bottlenecks.title: 24h retention storage exhaustion from sustained burst or replay
bottlenecks.trigger: 24h retention at sustained 5.8K tweets/sec × 1KB ≈ 500GB/day; during an extended 3x burst day that's ~1.5TB, and with replication factor 3 the cluster needs ~4.5TB of hot disk — a multi-day burst or a backfill replay of a new sketch config can blow through provisioned broker storage
bottlenecks.symptom: Brokers hit disk-full, start rejecting produces with NotEnoughReplicasException, ingest API's disk spool activates, and oldest segments get force-deleted before the 24h window — breaking any in-flight Flink replay/backfill
bottlenecks.mitigation: Provision brokers for 3x sustained (~15TB with RF=3) to absorb burst days; enable tiered storage (Kafka 3.6+) to offload cold segments to S3 so retention becomes elastic; monitor log.retention.bytes per-topic as a hard ceiling rather than only time-based
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on broker log-disk usage > 70%, on kafka_log_size growth rate > 2x baseline for >1h, and on any LogSegmentDeletion happening before the 24h mark

bottlenecks.title: Random partitioning defeats Flink's keyBy(country) locality
bottlenecks.trigger: Producer uses random partitioning (intentional, to avoid hot hashtags), but Flink does keyBy(country) downstream — every tweet gets network-shuffled to the subtask owning that country's key group, so at 18K peak tweets/sec essentially 100% of events cross the network between Flink operators
bottlenecks.symptom: Flink network buffers saturate under burst, backpressure propagates upstream to the Kafka source, and p99 end-to-end latency (ingest → cache) drifts from seconds into tens of seconds just as trending needs to be fresh
bottlenecks.mitigation: Partition Kafka by country (or country-hash-bucketed to avoid US/global skew) so Flink's keyBy becomes a local forward instead of a shuffle; accept the mild country-level skew as cheaper than a full shuffle of the firehose; keep hashtag-level aggregation within the country subtask where CMS handles skew naturally
bottlenecks.detection: Monitor Flink's numBytesInLocal vs numBytesInRemote ratio (should climb toward local-dominant after the fix), and alert on buffer-pool-usage > 80% sustained or backpressure > 0.5 on the source operator

prebuild.explanation: ### Why Kafka sits between ingest and Flink For a trending system riding a 500M-tweets/day firehose, you need a **durable buffer** that decouples the tweet write path from the analytics job. Flink is a stateful stream processor — it can crash, restart, or need to replay the last hour to rebuild a sketch after a config change. If tweets flowed directly from the Ingest API into Flink, any Flink hiccup would either drop tweets on the floor or push backpressure all the way into the user-visible write path. Kafka's 24h retention turns "Flink is down for 10 minutes" into a non-event: it just resumes from its last offset and catches up. ### What happens without it Without Kafka, a Flink checkpoint stall or a bad deploy means either (a) the trending panel goes stale for hours because there's no way to replay the tweets you missed, or (b) the Ingest API's disk spool overflows and starts dropping events silently. Operators would see trending topics frozen during exactly the breaking-news moments users care about — with no way to recover the lost window. ### The number Peak load is ~18K tweets/sec across 50 partitions = **~360 msgs/sec per partition**, well within Kafka's comfort zone (a single partition can handle 10K+/sec). At ~1KB per tweet, 24h retention costs `18K × 1KB × 86,400s ≈ 1.5TB/day`, or ~4.5TB with replication factor 3 — cheap insurance for a full day of replay capability. ### Trade-off The designer accepted an extra hop (and the ops cost of running a Kafka cluster) to get replayability and isolation between the write path and analytics.

flink.name: Stream Processor (Flink)
flink.summary: Consumes tweets, extracts tokens, maintains CMS + Top-K per 5-min sliding window.

sections.heading: Job DAG
sections.body: `Source(Kafka) → FlatMap(extractHashtags) → KeyBy(country) → SlidingWindow(5min,10s) → CMS+HeavyKeeper → Sink(cache + audit topic)`

sections.heading: Why Flink (not Spark Streaming)
sections.body: True per-event processing with event-time watermarks — matters when late tweets arrive from lagging regions. Spark micro-batches add 1–10s latency that's fine for dashboards but loose for trending.

sections.heading: State + checkpointing
sections.body: CMS + Top-K state is checkpointed to S3 every 60s. On crash, resume from last checkpoint (≤60s of re-read from Kafka).

sections.heading: Scaling
sections.body: Parallelism = 50 (one subtask per Kafka partition). Each subtask keeps ~16MB CMS state → 800MB across the cluster, easy for any Flink deployment.

lost: Event-time handling is less native than Flink

gained: No separate cluster — runs as a library in JVM apps
lost: Harder to scale state beyond a single consumer group

bottlenecks.title: Checkpoint stalls on S3 under 3x burst cause consumer-lag cascade
bottlenecks.trigger: 60s checkpoint interval writing ~800MB of CMS+Top-K state (50 subtasks × 16MB) to S3; during 3x burst (~36K tokens/sec) S3 PUT latency spikes or a single slow subtask stalls the aligned-checkpoint barrier, blocking the whole job for 30–120s
bottlenecks.symptom: Flink consumer-lag climbs into the millions, cache writes pause, trending panel freezes for 2–5 min exactly during breaking-news events; on-call sees checkpoint_duration p99 > 60s and backpressure=1.0 on all operators
bottlenecks.mitigation: Enable unaligned checkpoints so barriers overtake in-flight records; switch to incremental RocksDB checkpoints so only deltas ship to S3 (shrinks 16MB→KB per subtask); stretch checkpoint interval to 120s and set checkpoint-timeout=180s; use a dedicated S3 bucket with higher request-rate quota
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on lastCheckpointDuration p95 > 30s, checkpoint-failure-count > 0 in 5 min, or numberOfInProgressCheckpoints > 1 (indicates overlap/stall)

bottlenecks.title: Sliding-window ring of 30 sub-windows drives state explosion and GC
bottlenecks.trigger: 5-min window with 10s slide = 30 sub-window CMS instances kept in memory per key (country); with ~200 countries × 50 parallelism × 30 sub-windows × 16MB CMS, naive implementation blows past 800MB baseline into tens of GB and triggers long JVM GC pauses during the 10s rotation tick
bottlenecks.symptom: Periodic 10s-aligned latency spikes visible in currentEmitEventTimeLag; task manager OOMKilled or Full GC pauses >5s; Flink job restarts every few hours from checkpoint, each restart re-reading up to 60s of Kafka backlog
bottlenecks.mitigation: Use RocksDB state backend (not heap) so sub-window CMSes spill to local SSD; share a single CMS per sub-window across countries with (country,token) as the hash input; or switch to an incremental sliding CMS (Datar-Gionis-Indyk exponential histogram) that avoids keeping 30 full copies
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on task-manager heap usage > 75% sustained, GC pause-time p99 > 1s, or state-size growth rate > 100MB/min per subtask

bottlenecks.title: Event-time skew from lagging regions inflates watermarks and delays window emission
bottlenecks.trigger: keyBy(country) plus event-time watermarks means the slowest Kafka partition (e.g. a region with network lag or a producer-side backlog) holds back the global watermark; a single lagging partition at even 30s behind delays every 10s window emission for all countries
bottlenecks.symptom: Cache writes arrive late (generated_at drifts 30–60s behind wall clock), client RUM fires the 'updated Xs ago' warning, yet Flink metrics show no backpressure — the job is 'healthy' but outputs are stale
bottlenecks.mitigation: Use withIdleness(30s) on the Kafka source so idle/slow partitions don't hold back watermarks; set bounded out-of-orderness to 10s and route late events to a side output rather than waiting; monitor per-partition watermark lag and alert before it affects emission
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on max(currentInputWatermark) - min(currentInputWatermark) across subtasks > 20s, or on (wall_clock - output_watermark) > 30s for >2 min

prebuild.explanation: ### Why Flink is here for trending topics For a trending system over a 500M-tweets/day firehose, *something* has to sit between the raw Kafka stream and the Redis cache and do the actual counting — extract hashtags, maintain per-country sliding windows, and keep the Top-K updated every 10 seconds. Flink is that something. The reason it's Flink specifically (and not Spark Streaming or a cron job hitting a database) is **event-time windowing with watermarks**. Tweets arrive out of order — a tweet from a lagging region can show up 30 seconds late — and Flink can still place it in the correct 5-minute window instead of the window it happened to arrive in. That's the difference between "US trending at 8:00pm" being *actually* what was trending at 8:00pm versus a blurry approximation. ### What happens without it Without a stateful stream processor, you'd be stuck doing batch jobs (trending updates every few minutes with visible lag) or trying to maintain counts in Redis directly — which turns every hashtag into a hot key and melts your cache under the firehose. Users would see a trending panel that's always 2–3 minutes stale, and operators would see Redis CPU pegged on `INCR` storms during breaking news. ### The number At **18K peak tweets/sec × 2 hashtags = 36K tokens/sec**, Flink's 50 parallel subtasks handle ~720 tokens/sec each — each subtask holds a 16MB CMS in local state and updates it in-memory, no network round-trip per token. That's why the whole cluster fits in 800MB of state. ### Trade-off The designer accepted running a separate Flink cluster (ops overhead, checkpoint tuning) to get sub-second, event-time-correct windowing that a simpler batch or Redis-only design can't deliver.

cms.name: CMS + Top-K State
cms.summary: Approximate counting structures kept as Flink operator state.

sections.heading: Count-Min Sketch (CMS)
sections.body: `d x w` table of counters. For each token: hash with d independent hash functions, increment one counter per row. Query: take min across the d counters → overestimates at most ε * total with probability 1-δ. Params here: d=4, w=2^20 → ε ≈ 0.0001% of firehose, δ ≈ 1/16.

sections.heading: Top-K (HeavyKeeper or SpaceSaving)
sections.body: HeavyKeeper heap of size K=50; evicts with probability inversely proportional to counter. Correctness guarantee: every true heavy hitter above the 1/K threshold is found, with small chance of a false positive near the boundary.

sections.heading: Sliding window
sections.body: Maintained as ring of 30 sub-windows of 10s each; total window = 5 min. On each 10s tick: rotate out the oldest sub-window, merge others.

sections.heading: Why approximate over exact
sections.body: Exact counts require a map of 10M+ unique hashtags per window → GB of RAM + cross-node shuffles. CMS gives 99.99% accuracy for heavy hitters in 16MB. The long tail (rare terms) is noisy but we never show those anyway.

lost: Measures unique set size, not frequency — doesn't rank heavy hitters

alternatives.name: Exact counting with Redis Sorted Sets

lost: Write QPS into one Redis key becomes a hot shard

gained: Deduplicates bot-spam storms before they inflate trends

bottlenecks.title: CMS error floor swamps mid-tier hashtags during burst
bottlenecks.trigger: CMS error is ε × total_count; at 3x burst ~36K tokens/sec over a 5-min window that's ~10.8M tokens, so with w=2^20 the per-counter noise floor is ~10 counts — any hashtag with true count <100 in the window has >10% relative error, and two mid-rank hashtags near the K=50 boundary can swap places purely from hash collisions with the heavy hitters
bottlenecks.symptom: Trending list churns at positions 30–50 between 10s ticks even though no real ranking change occurred; product managers notice 'trending' showing obscure terms during a Super Bowl because a heavy-hitter's hash collided onto them; long-tail per-country trends (small countries with low token volume) show visibly wrong rankings
bottlenecks.mitigation: Bump width to w=2^22 (64MB per subtask, still trivial) to cut ε by 4x; enforce a minimum-count threshold (e.g. 0.1% of window total) before a topic is eligible for Top-K so collision-inflated rare terms can't surface; use Conservative Update (only increment the min counter row) which empirically cuts error 2–4x at no extra memory
bottlenecks.detection: Offline: periodically run exact counting on a 1% sampled sub-stream and compare Top-K Jaccard to CMS Top-K; alert when overlap <0.9. Online: alert on Top-K churn rate (positions changed per 10s tick) > 30% sustained for >2 min

bottlenecks.title: Sliding-window ring of 30 sub-CMSes multiplies memory and merge cost
bottlenecks.trigger: 5-min window with 10s slide requires 30 sub-window CMS instances per key-group; at 16MB each × 50 subtasks that's 24GB baseline (not the documented 800MB which ignored the ring), and every 10s tick must merge 30 sketches (d=4, w=2^20 = 16M counter additions per merge × 50 subtasks = 800M adds) on a single operator thread
bottlenecks.symptom: Periodic 10s-aligned CPU spikes and latency hiccups visible in currentEmitEventTimeLag; task-manager heap pressure leading to Full GC pauses >1s; state-size metric grows to tens of GB instead of the promised sub-GB, surprising ops during capacity planning
bottlenecks.mitigation: Replace the ring-of-30 with a single incremental sliding CMS (exponential-histogram-style, Datar-Gionis-Indyk) that maintains only O(log window) state per counter; or share one CMS per sub-window across all countries keyed by (country,token) so the 30x multiplier applies once globally instead of per key-group; store sub-window CMSes in RocksDB state backend so they spill to SSD
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on operator state-size > 2GB per subtask, on 10s-periodic GC pause-time p99 > 500ms, and on window-merge latency (custom metric emitted before/after merge) > 2s

bottlenecks.title: HeavyKeeper Top-K misses flash-rising hashtags at window boundaries
bottlenecks.trigger: HeavyKeeper's probabilistic eviction is inversely proportional to counter value, so a flash-rising hashtag (breaking-news spike) that starts mid-window must outpace incumbents already holding high counters from earlier in the 5-min window; with K=50 and incumbents at tens of thousands of counts, a new hashtag needs thousands of events in one 10s sub-window to have a meaningful eviction probability
bottlenecks.symptom: Breaking-news hashtags appear in trending 1–2 minutes later than they should, exactly when freshness matters most; users tweeting about a live event don't see their hashtag trend until well after it's peaked; competitors' trending panels surface the topic first
bottlenecks.mitigation: Maintain a parallel 'rising' Top-K keyed on delta (current sub-window count vs prior sub-window count) alongside the absolute-count Top-K, and blend both into the emitted list with a rising-boost weight; tune HeavyKeeper's decay parameter b down (more aggressive eviction) so stale incumbents fade within 1–2 sub-windows after their burst ends
bottlenecks.detection: Track per-hashtag first-seen-in-stream timestamp vs first-appeared-in-Top-K timestamp; alert when the p95 gap for hashtags that ultimately reach Top-10 exceeds 90s. Also monitor Top-K stability (fraction of topics unchanged across a 1-min span) — suspicious if >95% during a known breaking event

prebuild.explanation: ### Why approximate counting sits at the heart of this pipeline For a trending system over a 500M-tweets/day firehose, the hard question is: *how do you rank the top 50 hashtags out of millions of distinct ones, updated every 10 seconds, across a stream you can't pause?* The obvious answer — keep a `HashMap<hashtag, count>` — doesn't survive contact with the numbers. You'd have tens of millions of distinct hashtags per window (most of them typos, bot spam, or one-off phrases), each entry eating memory, and you'd need to either shuffle every increment across Flink nodes or keep a giant map per node. The Count-Min Sketch replaces that unbounded map with a **fixed-size `4 × 2^20` array of counters** that answers "how often have I seen this token?" with bounded error, and the HeavyKeeper/Top-K heap tracks just the 50 hashtags that actually matter. ### What happens without it Without sketches, Flink's state grows with the *long tail* of hashtags, not the popular ones. On a breaking-news day (Super Bowl, election), unique-token count explodes — tens of GB of operator state, RocksDB thrashing to SSD, checkpoint durations blow past 60s, and the job falls behind. Users see a trending panel frozen on yesterday's list; operators see consumer lag climbing into the millions. ### The number At peak, **36K tokens/sec × 300s window ≈ 10.8M tokens** flowing through one window. An exact map of unique terms might hold ~10M entries at ~50 bytes each = **500MB per subtask × 50 subtasks = 25GB**. The CMS does it in `4 × 2^20 × 4B = 16MB` per subtask — a **1500× reduction** — while still nailing every heavy hitter within a few percent. ### The trade-off The designer accepted unreliable counts for the long tail (which nobody displays anyway) in exchange for fitting the entire ranking problem into in-memory operator state.

cache.name: Hot Topic Cache
cache.summary: Redis holding precomputed trending lists per country.

sections.heading: What's stored
sections.body: `trending:{country}` → JSON list of top 20 topics with rank/score/delta. Written by Flink sink every 10s.

sections.heading: Why a cache (not DB)
sections.body: Reads dwarf writes (120 RPS reads vs 1 write per 10s per country). Keeping it in Redis makes reads sub-ms and survives even if Flink is briefly down — trending just gets stale.

sections.heading: TTL
sections.body: None — Flink overwrites every 10s. If Flink stops publishing, a separate watchdog fires an alert at 2 min of staleness.

bottlenecks.title: Thundering herd on single country key during breaking news
bottlenecks.trigger: Breaking-news event causes CDN cache miss on `trending:US` (the 30s CDN TTL expires exactly when millions of clients are polling); Trending API fleet converges on a single Redis key with correlated GETs — at 3x burst this can drive 10K+ concurrent GETs against one key on one Redis shard
bottlenecks.symptom: Redis CPU on the shard owning `trending:US` pegs at 100%, GET p99 climbs from <1ms into tens of ms, Trending API connection pool saturates waiting on Redis, and 5xx rate on /trending spikes exactly during the breaking-news moment
bottlenecks.mitigation: Add request coalescing at the Trending API (single-flight per country key so only one request per replica hits Redis on CDN miss); replicate Redis with 2–3 read replicas and route reads round-robin; stagger CDN TTLs per country (±5s jitter) so global keys don't expire in lockstep; keep an in-process LRU in the API with 5s TTL as a last line of defense
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on Redis per-key hit rate skew (one key >50% of GETs), on Redis instantaneous_ops_per_sec > 50K on any shard, and on Trending API redis-wait-time p99 > 10ms

bottlenecks.title: Silent staleness when Flink sink pauses writes
bottlenecks.trigger: Flink checkpoint stall, job restart (≤60s Kafka re-read), or sink backpressure pauses the 10s cache-write cadence; because keys have no TTL, Redis happily serves the last-written JSON indefinitely — the documented 2-min watchdog alert is the only backstop
bottlenecks.symptom: Trending panel shows a frozen list for minutes during an active event; users complain the product is broken; generated_at timestamp embedded in the JSON drifts well past 90s client-side threshold, triggering RUM staleness alerts before the server-side watchdog fires
bottlenecks.mitigation: Embed generated_at in every cached value and have the Trending API compare it to wall clock — serve with a staleness header when >60s old and return 503 (or hide the panel) when >5 min; tighten the watchdog from 2 min to 45s; add a dead-man's-switch key `trending:heartbeat` that Flink refreshes every 10s and alert if it goes stale
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on max(now - generated_at) across all country keys > 60s for >1 min; alert on Flink sink-write-count to Redis dropping to 0 for >30s; client RUM p95 staleness > 90s

bottlenecks.title: Redis single-node failure drops all trending reads
bottlenecks.trigger: Single Redis primary handles all country keys (~200 keys × few KB = KB-scale, so no sharding pressure exists to force a cluster); an AZ outage, OOM from a misconfigured MEMORY command, or a Redis version upgrade takes the node down and there's no documented failover path
bottlenecks.symptom: 100% of /trending requests miss cache simultaneously, Trending API has no fallback source (Flink writes to cache, not DB), so requests 5xx for the full failover window (30s–2min); CDN absorbs some load via stale-while-revalidate but most clients see spinners
bottlenecks.mitigation: Run Redis Sentinel or Redis Cluster with a replica in a second AZ (automatic failover in <30s); have the Trending API fall back to serving stale CDN content with extended max-age on Redis 5xx; configure Flink sink to write to both primary and a warm standby cache so failover doesn't lose the last 10s of state
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on Redis availability <100% over 1 min, on Trending API cache-miss-rate > 5% (should be ~0% in steady state), and on replica-lag > 1s between primary and standby

prebuild.explanation: ### Why there's a cache between Flink and the read API For a trending-topics system over a 500M-tweets/day firehose, the Hot Topic Cache is the **handoff point** between the streaming world (Flink, sketches, windows) and the request-response world (users tapping the trending panel). Flink is great at counting, but it's not a database — you can't point a user-facing API at a Flink operator and ask "what's trending in the US right now?" thousands of times a second. So Flink *writes* its answer to Redis every 10 seconds, and the API *reads* from Redis. That seam also means the read path keeps working even if Flink is briefly down — the list just gets stale rather than disappearing. ### What happens without it If the Trending API queried Flink (or recomputed from Kafka) on every request, every panel open would trigger a heavy stateful lookup into the stream processor. Users would see multi-second spinners, Flink operators would get hammered with read RPCs that compete with ingest, and a Flink restart (≤60s Kafka re-read) would take the whole trending feature down instead of just freezing the displayed list. ### The number Reads dwarf writes here: **~120 read RPS** (`10M reads/day ÷ 86,400s`) versus **1 write per 10s per country** ≈ 0.1 writes/sec per key. Redis serves those reads in sub-millisecond time from RAM, and since the payload is KB-scale per country, the whole working set fits comfortably in a single node's memory. ### Trade-off The designer accepted up-to-10s staleness in the displayed list in exchange for decoupling reads from the stream processor entirely.

api.name: Trending API
api.summary: Thin read API returning the trending list for a country.

sections.heading: Endpoint
sections.body: `GET /trending?country=US&limit=20` → `[{topic, rank, score, delta_pct, sample_tweets}]`

sections.heading: Caching layers
sections.body: Redis is already in-memory; CDN caches the JSON response for 30s to absorb any traffic spikes (e.g. breaking news).

sections.heading: Scaling
sections.body: 120 RPS is trivial; 2 replicas handle it. CDN absorbs spikes.

bottlenecks.title: CDN cache miss stampede collapses the 2-replica fleet
bottlenecks.trigger: Breaking-news event (Super Bowl, election call) drives correlated panel opens; the CDN's 30s TTL expires simultaneously across edge POPs and millions of clients poll within the same second. Baseline is ~120 RPS but a 100x correlated burst pushes origin load into the 10K+ RPS range against only 2 replicas sized for 120 RPS (concurrency=2000 per replica).
bottlenecks.symptom: Trending API p99 latency blows past the 100ms SLO into seconds, 5xx rate climbs, clients retry-tap making it worse, and the trending panel shows spinners exactly during the breaking-news moment users care about most.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Enable CDN stale-while-revalidate (serve-stale for up to 5min on origin 5xx); add ±5s jitter to CDN TTLs per country key so global keys don't expire in lockstep; implement single-flight request coalescing per (country,limit) tuple at the API so only one Redis GET per replica fires on miss; raise min replicas to 4 with HPA on CPU>50% and 60s scale-out target.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on Trending API RPS > 10x rolling 1h baseline within 1min, on CDN origin-fetch ratio > 5% (hit ratio should stay >95% for a 30s-cached JSON), and on p99 latency > 50ms for >1min.

bottlenecks.title: Serving silently stale data when Flink sink pauses
bottlenecks.trigger: Flink checkpoint stall or job restart (≤60s Kafka re-read documented) pauses the 10s cache-write cadence; Redis keys have no TTL so the API happily returns the last-written JSON indefinitely, and the watchdog alert only fires at 2min staleness.
bottlenecks.symptom: Users see a frozen trending list for minutes during an active news event; product appears broken exactly when freshness matters; on-call gets paged late because the API reports 200s with seemingly valid payloads.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Have the API read the embedded generated_at from the Redis JSON and compare to wall clock: attach an X-Trending-Staleness-Seconds response header always, add a soft warning in-body when staleness >60s, and return 503 (letting CDN serve-stale kick in) when >5min. Check a `trending:heartbeat` dead-man key on each request and fail fast if Flink has stopped writing.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on API-emitted metric max(now - generated_at) across served responses > 60s for >1min; track the fraction of responses with staleness-warning header > 0 as a SLI; page when >1% sustained.

bottlenecks.title: sample_tweets payload bloat burns CDN bandwidth and mobile TTFB
bottlenecks.trigger: Response shape is `[{topic, rank, score, delta_pct, sample_tweets}]` with limit=20; at a few KB per sample tweet this balloons to 50–100KB per response. With 10M reads/day and 30s CDN caching, origin bandwidth is fine but edge→client bandwidth scales with every poll on mobile networks.
bottlenecks.symptom: Elevated mobile data-usage complaints, slow panel render on 3G/Lie-Fi, p99 client-observed latency well above the 100ms target (mostly network transfer, not server time), and CDN egress cost climbs disproportionately to request count.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Split the API: the list endpoint returns only `{topic, rank, score, delta_pct}` (~2KB for 20 items), and a separate `/trending/{topic}/samples` endpoint lazy-loads sample tweets when a user expands a topic. Enable brotli at the CDN, cap limit<=20 server-side with 400 on larger requests, and set Vary: Accept-Encoding.
bottlenecks.detection: Histogram of response Content-Length by endpoint; alert when p95 list-endpoint payload > 5KB or p95 gzipped > 2KB. RUM metric on mobile TTFB p95 > 300ms.

prebuild.explanation: ### Why there's a thin API in front of the cache For a trending topics system over a 500M-tweets/day firehose, the Trending API is the **boundary between the public internet and the analytics internals**. Flink is busy counting hashtags, Redis holds the precomputed list, but neither of those should be exposed directly to millions of mobile clients. The API is where you put authentication, rate limiting, response shaping (trimming to `limit=20`, picking the right country), and — critically — the CDN cache-control headers that let a 30s-cached JSON absorb traffic spikes before they ever reach Redis. ### What happens without it If clients talked to Redis directly, every panel open would open a Redis connection from an untrusted device. Redis connection counts would explode during breaking-news events, one malformed client could hammer a single country key, and you'd have no place to sit the CDN layer that protects the cache from stampedes. Operators would see Redis CPU pegged and have no knobs to turn — no way to shed load, no way to version the response shape, no way to roll out a new field without a Redis schema migration. ### The number Baseline read load is `10M reads/day ÷ 86,400s ≈ 120 RPS`. That's trivial — 2 replicas handle it easily. But the API's real job is absorbing the **100× correlated burst** during events (10K+ RPS) via its CDN layer, so the 2-replica fleet never sees more than a trickle of origin misses. ### Trade-off The designer accepted an extra network hop (~3–10ms) to get a controllable, cacheable, rate-limitable seam between users and the stream processor.

operations.title: Tweet enters the analytics pipeline
operations.name: Tweet enters the analytics pipeline
operations.description: Tweet write path publishes to Kafka; does not block user write.

steps.title: Ingest adapter receives a tweet event from the core write path
steps.action: The core Twitter write service fires a post-commit hook that POSTs the canonical tweet event to the analytics Ingest API. The adapter validates the schema, normalizes the timestamp to UTC epoch-ms, and hands the record to the async Kafka producer. Importantly, the response to the caller is decoupled from the Kafka ack — a 50ms send timeout falls back to the local disk spool so a Kafka hiccup never stalls user tweeting.

incoming.label: Tweet event (HTTP POST from write path)

steps.note: The producer uses acks=1 (leader only) rather than acks=all. Analytics durability tolerates the rare single-broker-loss window in exchange for half the produce latency — this is an explicit trade-off documented on the Ingest component.

steps.title: Kafka broker appends record to the tweets topic
steps.action: The producer's partitioner selects a random partition (no key) to avoid hot hashtags collapsing onto a single partition. The partition leader appends the record to its log segment, replicates to 2 followers (RF=3), and acknowledges once the leader write is durable. 24h retention means Flink can replay from any offset in the last day if it crashes or needs to rebuild a sketch.
steps.codeOrCommand:
# Broker-side append (conceptual)
part = partitioner.pick(topic="tweets", key=None) # sticky-random → P37
leader = metadata["tweets"][37].leader # broker-12
leader.log.append(offset=next, record=rec)
replicate_to(followers=[broker-08, broker-21])
ack_to_producer(offset=18_472_991_204)
steps.note: Flink's source operator for partition 37 is subscribed via consumer group `trending-job-v3` and will pick up this offset on its next poll (typically within 50–100ms). The tweet is now durable in Kafka; the ingest API has long since returned 200 to the caller.

operations.title: Stream processor updates sketches
operations.name: Stream processor updates sketches
operations.description: Flink consumes, extracts hashtags, updates CMS + Top-K, periodically publishes to cache.

steps.title: Flink source polls the next batch from its assigned partitions
steps.action: Each of Flink's 50 source subtasks is pinned 1:1 to a Kafka partition. The subtask for P37 issues a fetch request against the broker starting at its last-committed offset and receives a batch of records (up to `fetch.max.bytes=1MB` or `max.poll.records=500`, whichever comes first). The batch is handed downstream to the FlatMap operator.
steps.codeOrCommand:
# Flink KafkaSource config (Java-ish pseudocode)
KafkaSource<TweetEvent> src = KafkaSource.<TweetEvent>builder.setBootstrapServers("kafka-analytics:9092").setTopics("tweets").setGroupId("trending-job-v3").setStartingOffsets(OffsetsInitializer.committedOffsets).setValueOnlyDeserializer(new AvroTweetDeserializer).build; # per-subtask fetch (broker side)
records = broker.fetch(partition=37, offset=18472990712, max_bytes=1_048_576)
# returns 493 records including our tweet at offset 18472991204

steps.title: FlatMap tokenizes hashtags; keyBy(country) routes into windowed CMS operator
steps.action: The source hands each record to a FlatMap that emits one (country, hashtag, ts) record per hashtag in the tweet — our sample tweet fans out into two downstream records for `#SuperBowl` and `#Halftime`. Records are then keyed by country, assigned event-time watermarks, and bucketed into the active 10s sub-window. Using keyBy(country) means all hashtag updates for a country land in the same subtask, so CMS updates are purely local and never cross the network.
steps.note: withIdleness(30s) prevents a quiet region from holding back the global watermark — without it, one slow Kafka partition would delay every 10s window emission worldwide.

steps.title: CmsTopKFunction updates Count-Min Sketch and HeavyKeeper heap for the current sub-window
steps.action: For each token, the operator hashes with d=4 independent functions, increments the addressed counter in each of the 4 rows (using Conservative Update — only the row with the minimum current value is incremented to tighten error), then queries the min across rows as the point-estimate and feeds it into a K=50 HeavyKeeper heap. The sub-window this sample belongs to is the one covering `[22:17:00, 22:17:10)`; a ring of 30 such sub-windows represents the full 5-min sliding view. On every 10s tick the operator rotates: merge all 30 sub-CMSes into a view-CMS, extract the top 50, emit to the sink.
steps.decision: No Top-K eviction this event — both tokens were already heavy hitters above the K=50 boundary. If a flash-rising tag with current count > heap-minimum had arrived, HeavyKeeper would probabilistically evict the weakest incumbent.
steps.note: Conservative Update (only increment rows currently at the min) is a free accuracy win — empirically cuts ε by 2–4x at no memory cost vs textbook CMS.

steps.title: On 10s tick, Flink sink flushes the per-country Top-K to Redis
steps.action: Separately from per-token processing, a ProcessingTimeTimer fires every 10 seconds. It asks the CmsTopKFunction for each country's current merged Top-K (30 sub-CMSes merged into one view, heap extracted), formats it as a JSON payload with rank/score/delta_pct vs the prior 10s tick, and issues a single Redis SET per country. A dead-man heartbeat key is refreshed in the same pipeline so downstream watchdogs can detect a stalled sink.
steps.note: This sink runs in parallel with (not blocking) per-event CMS updates — the 10s timer owns its own invocation slot on the operator thread. If Redis is slow or briefly down, the sink queues writes; the CMS state is the source of truth.

operations.title: Read trending list
operations.name: Read trending list
operations.description: User opens trending panel; API serves precomputed list from Redis (falls back to reading the latest CMS snapshot from Flink state on cache miss).

steps.title: User opens the trending panel in the app
steps.action: The mobile client renders the Trending tab and issues a GET for the user's home-country list. Poll cadence is 30–60s with ±25% jitter to decorrelate clients during breaking-news events. The request carries an If-None-Match header against the ETag from the last response so the CDN can answer 304 Not Modified when nothing has changed.
steps.note: Jitter is critical — without it, a tab-focus event on millions of phones can produce a correlated 10K+ RPS spike against the Trending API at the exact moment the CDN TTL expires.

steps.title: Trending API authenticates, validates country, and issues a single Redis GET
steps.action: The API terminates TLS at the CDN (pass-through to origin on miss), validates the country code is ISO-3166 alpha-2, clamps limit to [1,20], and — after single-flight request coalescing per (country,limit) tuple — issues one Redis GET for `trending:US`. Request coalescing means that even if 500 concurrent requests hit this replica on a CDN miss, only one Redis call fires per replica.

incoming.label: HTTP GET (origin fetch after CDN miss)

steps.codeOrCommand:
# Trending API handler (Python-ish)
if country not in ISO_3166: return 400
limit = min(max(int(limit or 20), 1), 20) # single-flight: coalesce concurrent identical requests
key = f"sf:{country}:{limit}"
fut = single_flight.do(key, lambda: redis.get(f"trending:{country}"))
raw = fut.result(timeout=0.080) # 80ms cap

steps.title: Redis returns the precomputed trending JSON
steps.action: Redis performs an O(1) hash-table lookup on the key and returns the last value written by the Flink sink — typically within the last 10 seconds. The embedded generated_at field lets the API detect staleness if Flink's sink has paused. This is the hot path: 99%+ of reads are served here in sub-millisecond time.
steps.codeOrCommand:
GET trending:US
# internal: dict.lookup("trending:US") → slot 0x7a1e → value bytes
steps.decision: HIT — value present and fresh (age 1.84s << 60s soft threshold). Return it. On a MISS (Flink sink stalled / Redis failover mid-write), the API's fallback path issues a Flink Queryable-State RPC (`ZREVRANGE`-style call against the live CmsTopKFunction state) to read the current merged Top-K directly from the stream processor; that path is 20–50ms instead of sub-ms but keeps the panel alive during Redis outages.
steps.note: Alternative-design sibling: an exact-counting design would store topics in a Redis Sorted Set and serve reads via `ZREVRANGE trending:US 0 19 WITHSCORES` — same client-visible latency, but the write-side hot-key problem makes it infeasible at 36K tokens/sec (documented in the cms component's alternatives).

steps.title: API shapes the response, attaches staleness + ETag headers
steps.action: The API truncates to `limit`, computes `X-Trending-Staleness-Seconds = now - generated_at`, and attaches a weak ETag derived from generated_at so clients can cheaply re-check via If-None-Match. If staleness > 60s a soft warning is included in the body; if > 5min the API returns 503 and lets the CDN's stale-while-revalidate serve the last known good response.
steps.codeOrCommand:
payload = json.loads(raw)
top = payload['top'][:limit]
age_s = (now_ms - payload['generated_at']) / 1000 headers = { 'Content-Type': 'application/json', 'Cache-Control': 'public, max-age=30, stale-while-revalidate=300', 'ETag': f'W/"{payload["generated_at"]}"', 'X-Trending-Staleness-Seconds': f'{age_s:.1f}', 'Vary': 'Accept-Encoding'
}
if age_s > 300: return 503, headers
if age_s > 60: payload['warnings'] = ['stale'] return 200, headers, json.dumps({ 'country': country, 'generated_at': payload['generated_at'], 'topics': top
})

steps.title: Client renders the list and schedules the next jittered poll
steps.action: The client parses the JSON, diffs against the previously rendered list to animate rank changes, and displays an 'updated Xs ago' label derived from generated_at. It stores the new ETag for the next If-None-Match and schedules the next poll at `base + jitter` where base is 45s and jitter is ±25%. If the response carried a staleness warning or the client's own (now - generated_at) exceeds 90s, the client shortens the next poll to 10s to recover quickly.
steps.note: End-to-end perceived latency on the hot path is typically 20–60ms: CDN edge (1–5ms) + origin pass-through on miss + Redis (sub-ms) + response body over mobile network. The CDN absorbs ~95% of requests so origin only sees the ~120 RPS baseline even during breaking-news bursts.

tradeoffs.rationale: Fixed memory per window and single-pass updates with bounded over-counting. Exact counts would require a global counter per distinct term and cross-node shuffling, which does not scale to a firehose.

tradeoffs.chosen: MinHeap of size K keyed by estimated count
tradeoffs.rationale: Amortized O(log K) per update and a trivial snapshot operation. Cost is a map plus heap per task, but K is small (tens) so the overhead is negligible.
Matches human perception of "trending" while keeping stream state small. Tighter windows increase snapshot pressure on the cache and the CMS error rate for short-lived spikes.

tradeoffs.chosen: Hot topic cache keyed by window_end_ts
tradeoffs.rationale: Keeps the read API stateless and lets the CDN cache the JSON for tens of seconds. The tradeoff is that any correction to a snapshot requires publishing a new key rather than mutating an existing one.

tradeoffs.chosen: Async producer with local disk spool on Kafka slowdown
tradeoffs.rationale: Analytics must never block user-visible tweeting. Accepts the risk of dropping analytics events on extended Kafka outage in exchange for zero back-pressure on the write path.

interviewFollowUps.question: Add per-language and per-country heavy-hitter streams with a merge step at read time
Detect spam / bot amplification and exclude flagged accounts before they feed the sketch
Introduce a personalized trending overlay by joining heavy hitters with a user's follow graph
Replace the fixed 5-minute window with an adaptive window that shortens during bursty events
Add a cold analytics path that writes exact counts to a warehouse for backfill and correctness audits
